meta.descriptionEn: A 19-year-old Stanford dropout promised a revolution: many medical tests from a single finger-prick. Elizabeth Holmes built Theranos into a company valued at $9 billion, surrounded by former secretaries of state, generals and powerful investors. Pharmacies signed deals, magazines put her on their covers, and she modeled her style on Steve Jobs. Then a Wall Street Journal reporter, a young whistleblower and a handful of regulators began asking uncomfortable questions. What were the machines really doing? Why did so many smart people believe? And how did it all fall apart? This documentary traces the rise, the warning signs, the investigation, the trials and the lessons Silicon Valley is still learning.
meta.descriptionUr: Ek 19 saal ki Stanford dropout ne dawa kiya ke sirf ek qatray se bohat se medical tests ho sakte hain. Elizabeth Holmes ki company Theranos ki qeemat 9 billion dollar tak pohanch gayi, aur uske board par purane wazeer, generals aur arab-pati investors thay. Phir ek reporter, ek jawan whistleblower aur regulators ne sawal uthaye. Machines asal mein kya kar rahi thin? Itne samajhdar log kyun dhoke mein aaye? Aur yeh sab kaise bikhra? Is documentary mein poori kahani dekhein, Urdu aur English mein.

articleEn: On 3 January 2022, a jury in a US court found Elizabeth Holmes guilty on four counts. She had once been counted among the most successful founders in the country. In November 2022 she was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in prison. But this story does not begin in a jail cell. It begins with a very big promise.

Her partner Sunny Balwani was found guilty on 12 counts in July 2022, and in December he received 12 years and 11 months in prison. The company was called Theranos. At one point its valuation reached 9 billion dollars, and it raised more than 700 million dollars from investors. In 2016 Forbes revised its estimate of Holmes's personal net worth from 4.5 billion dollars to zero. On paper, an entire empire had vanished.

So the questions are these. How did generals, billionaires and the media come to believe a promise of many tests from just a few drops of blood? Was any of the technology real? And where did the much-talked-about machines end up? A newspaper investigation then revealed that the company's own tests were often running on traditional machines made by other companies.

This documentary follows a college dropout, her famous board, the whistleblowers, the regulators and finally the court. Along the way we will look at what was true, what was false, and where people stopped asking questions. Let's begin at the beginning.

articleEn: Elizabeth Holmes was born on 3 February 1984 in Washington, D.C. She finished high school at St. John's School in Houston. Her father, Christian Holmes, later held senior posts at bodies such as USAID and the EPA, while her mother was a staffer on a Congressional committee. In high school she was interested in computer programming, and she says she started her first business by selling C++ compilers to Chinese universities.

In 2002 she arrived at Stanford University to study chemical engineering. After her first year she worked in a lab at the Genome Institute in Singapore, where SARS testing was carried out. In 2003 she filed her first patent application, for a wearable patch that could adjust the dose of a medicine and give doctors information about a patient's blood.

Then a bigger idea took hold: blood tests that were cheap, easy and within everyone's reach. In Holmes's words, she wanted to democratize healthcare. She also says her fear of needles was part of her motivation. Her aim was to get a wealth of data from just a few drops taken from a fingertip.

Sources differ on when she dropped out. One says she left Stanford in 2003, another says March 2004. Either way, she put the money set aside for her education into the company. It was first called Real-Time Cures and was based in Palo Alto. Holmes later felt that people were suspicious of the word "cure," so the name was changed to Theranos, a blend of the words therapy and diagnosis.

Not everyone was convinced. Phyllis Gardner, a Stanford medicine professor, told Holmes her idea would not work and that what she claimed was simply not possible. Several other medical professors told her the same. But Holmes did not back down. She won the support of her advisor Channing Robertson, dean of the School of Engineering. Robertson became the company's first board member and introduced her to venture capitalists.

That opened the road to funding. Tim Draper, a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and the father of a childhood friend of Holmes, became her first big investor. After hearing the pitch he wrote a check for 1 million dollars. By December 2004 Holmes had raised 6 million dollars. At the time the company was operating out of a rented basement near Stanford.

Ramesh Sunny Balwani was also part of her life. The two met in 2002 on a Stanford Mandarin program trip to Beijing. Balwani is 19 years older than Holmes. They became a couple in 2003 and began living together in 2005. Balwani officially became Theranos's president and COO in 2009, though he had been advising from the start.
Theranos now had an idea, a young founder and a trusted partner. But the experts' question remained: could the idea actually work?

articleEn: By the end of 2010, Theranos had raised more than 92 million dollars in venture capital. Money was flowing in. But the next turning point in the story came in July 2011, when Holmes was introduced to George Shultz, a former US Secretary of State. After a two-hour meeting he joined the Theranos board of directors. Over the following three years, Shultz helped bring in almost all of the outside directors.

The board was later called the most impressive in American corporate history. It included Henry Kissinger, former Defense Secretary William Perry, and former senators Sam Nunn and Bill Frist, each a big name in his field. Admiral Gary Roughead and Marine General Jim Mattis, who later became US Defense Secretary, were also members. So were Dick Kovacevich, the former CEO of Wells Fargo, and Riley Bechtel, the former CEO of Bechtel. Bechtel also served as chairman of the board. Critics did object, however, that most of these people came from diplomatic or military backgrounds.

In 2012 Safeway invested 350 million dollars to build clinics in 800 locations where blood tests would be offered. That deal ended in 2015. Throughout this period Holmes kept Theranos in stealth mode. Until September 2013 there was no press release and no company website. Then, in September 2013, a partnership with Walgreens was announced. The plan was to offer in-store blood tests at more than 40 locations.

Eric Topol, editor-in-chief of Medscape, interviewed Holmes and praised what he called a phenomenal rebooting of laboratory medicine. Media attention grew quickly. In 2014 Holmes appeared on the covers of Fortune, Forbes, T Magazine and Inc. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire in the world, and she ranked 110th on the Forbes 400. Most sources put Theranos's valuation at 9 billion dollars, though one source lists a peak of 10 billion. By the end of 2014 Holmes was named on 18 US patents and 66 foreign patents, which also added to the company's standing.
Holmes admired Steve Jobs and often wore a black turtleneck. According to one employee, she was advised in 2007 to adopt Jobs's look.

Long before Shultz, there was another name on the board: Tevanian. He left Apple on 31 March 2006 and joined the Theranos board. He resigned at the end of 2007. By his account, he often voiced doubts alone in board meetings about the company's finances and the progress of its technology. His departure was described as acrimonious. Tevanian faced legal threats and had to give up the right to buy a co-founder's shares. He believed this was retaliation.
So on one side stood a famous board, magazine covers and a valuation in the billions. On the other stood the same old question: does this technology really work? The answer would come out later.

articleEn: So what had Theranos told the world? The company claimed to have built blood tests that were both fast and accurate, and that needed very little blood. A single prick of the finger, and a small automated device would handle everything. The small vial for collecting blood was called the nanotainer. It was only 12.9 millimetres tall and held just a few drops. The analysis machine was called Edison, reportedly named by Holmes after the inventor Thomas Edison.

On paper, though, the system was not so clear. One Edison patent mentioned roughly 10 drops of blood in one place, while another part of the same patent said less than a single drop would be enough. In other words, its own documents contained two different claims. The patent also described an interesting idea: the device would receive instructions over the internet, send results back, and then run more targeted tests on its own. Remember, all of this was the company's claim. No independent proof of the tests' accuracy was available to the public.

Now consider an expert's concern. According to David Agus, blood clots, and in tiny fluidic channels the path gets blocked. Agus says Holmes did not answer this problem. For him that was the first red flag. He felt she was either extremely secretive or her explanations did not make sense.

The second big question was evidence. The company said it had accuracy data and would publish it. In February 2015, Stanford professor John Ioannidis raised exactly this point in JAMA, noting that no peer-reviewed research on Theranos existed. Then in May 2015, Eleftherios Diamandis of the University of Toronto reviewed Theranos's technology and concluded that most of the claims were exaggerated. But these voices were still few.

Meanwhile, big names kept attaching themselves to Theranos. In March 2015 the Cleveland Clinic announced a partnership, aiming to test the technology and lower the cost of lab tests. It was a major boost for the company. In July 2015 Theranos became the lab-work provider for the Pennsylvania insurers AmeriHealth Caritas and Capital Blue Cross. That same month the FDA approved the use of the company's fingerstick blood testing device outside a clinical laboratory for the herpes simplex virus test, HSV-1. This was genuine approval, but for only one test. The question about all the other tests remained. Reports said Theranos tests had also been used on patients in drug trials by GlaxoSmithKline and Pfizer, but in October 2015 both said they had no active projects.

Awards rained down in 2015. The Arizona BioIndustry Association named Theranos its 2015 Bioscience Company of the Year. Holmes herself made Time's 100 most influential people and became the youngest recipient of the Horatio Alger Award. Forbes ranked her the 73rd most powerful woman in 2015 and put her net worth at 4.5 billion dollars.
The picture, then, was praise, awards and big partnerships on one side, and claims without peer review on the other. And then a reporter began asking questions.

articleEn: The story now turns to a reporter and a young employee. John Carreyrou, an investigative journalist at the Wall Street Journal, was at the center of it. A medical expert had given him a tip: this expert found Theranos's Edison blood testing device suspicious. Carreyrou quietly investigated for several months. He spoke to former employees and obtained company documents.

One of his key sources was Tyler Shultz, who worked at Theranos from 2013 to 2014. Interestingly, he was the grandson of George Shultz, who was then a Theranos director. Tyler first took his concerns to company management. When that went nowhere, he spoke to Carreyrou. He also used a pseudonym to report CLIA violations to the New York State Department of Health.

When Holmes's lawyer David Boies learned of the investigation, Holmes launched an effort to stop it. The Journal and the whistleblowers were both threatened legally and financially. Theranos's lawyers also targeted sources like Tyler Shultz.

The company was also trying to boost its credibility. Holmes invited then Vice President Joe Biden for a tour of the facility, and Biden praised what he saw. But according to one source, Holmes and Balwani had built a fake lab to hide the real conditions.

Then came October 2015. The Wall Street Journal published Carreyrou's report, later called a bombshell article. According to the report, Theranos was using ordinary blood testing machines made by other companies, not Edison, for most of its tests. It also said Edison machines could give wrong results. So the problem was not only concealment but also the accuracy of the results.

Carreyrou kept reporting on Theranos and published the book Bad Blood in 2018. Theranos dismissed the allegations as factually and scientifically erroneous. Holmes called the Journal a tabloid. That evening she appeared on CNBC's Mad Money and promised the company would publish data on the accuracy of its tests. Jim Cramer said the article was pretty brutal. In reply, Holmes said that people who bring change are first thought crazy, then fought, and in the end they change the world. But the question remained: where was the test data?
After the report, Walgreens put its plans to expand blood-testing centers on hold. The Cleveland Clinic announced it would work on verifying Theranos's technology.

There is one more allegation. Former employees of a reputation management firm called Status Labs say Theranos hired them to quietly remove references to the WSJ's reporting from Theranos's Wikipedia article. That violated the site's terms of use.
Pressure on Theranos was now mounting. The journalist had spoken and the whistleblower had come forward. The next question was what the regulators would find.

articleEn: After October 2015, Theranos had to answer on many fronts. First came the FDA inspection reports. Reports from 2014 and 2015 stated that the blood collection containers had not been validated under actual or simulated use conditions. Then a debate arose over the nanotainer. The FDA classified it as a Class II medical device, which would require special labels, performance standards and post-market surveillance. Theranos's position was that the nanotainer was a Class I device, so no such regulatory requirements applied. The two positions were far apart. After the 2015 inspection, the company announced it was voluntarily suspending its other tests, apart from the FDA-approved HSV-1 test.

Then came January 2016. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, sent Theranos a letter based on its 2015 inspection of the Newark, California lab. The letter said the facility posed immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety. This concerned a test for dosing the blood thinner warfarin.

In March 2016, a study by 13 scientists appeared in the Journal of Clinical Investigation. It found notable differences between services in 68 percent of lab measurements. It also said Theranos results were flagged as outside the normal range 1.6 times more often than results from other services. CMS then signaled that it intended to impose sanctions, including barring Holmes and Balwani from owning or running a certified clinical laboratory for two years.

In May 2016, Theranos said it had voided two years of results from the Edison device. That same month Balwani left his post as president and COO. Holmes says she removed him, while Balwani says he left on his own. In June 2016 the company said roughly 1 percent of its machines' results had been voided or corrected. Within two weeks Walgreens ended the partnership.

In July 2016, CMS revoked Theranos's CLIA certificate. Holmes was barred from running a blood-testing service for two years. Approval for Medicare and Medicaid payments was suspended and a civil monetary penalty was imposed. Theranos announced an appeal. The FDA also ordered the company to stop using the Capillary Tube Nanotainer device, one of its core inventions.

In August 2016, Theranos introduced a new device called the miniLab but offered no data supporting its capabilities. That month the company also withdrew its request for emergency clearance of a Zika virus test, because federal inspectors found a lack of necessary safeguards. In October 2016, Theranos announced it was closing its lab operations and wellness centers. 340 people were laid off, and another 155 in January 2017.

Then came the Arizona matter. The state alleged that the company had hidden or misrepresented important facts while selling 1.5 million blood tests. In April 2017 Theranos reached a settlement. Arizona residents were refunded whether or not their results had been voided, for a total of 4.65 million dollars. That same month a settlement was also reached with CMS, in which the company agreed to stay out of the blood-testing business for at least two years. But the real storm was still to come.

articleEn: In May 2017, about 99 percent of shareholders reached an agreement with the company. All existing and potential claims were dropped, and in return they received new preferred shares. Holmes also gave up some of her own equity so that the value of shareholders who did not join would not be reduced.

In May 2018, John Carreyrou reported that big names in American business and government had lost more than 600 million dollars in Theranos. Major investments included 150 million from the Walton family, 121 million from Rupert Murdoch, 100 million from Betsy DeVos and 100 million from the Cox family. After the company was liquidated, all of these investments became worthless.

Before that, however, the company made one last attempt to stay alive. In December 2017, Fortress Investment Group lent Theranos 100 million dollars and took 4 percent of the company in return. The loan was secured by patents. In April 2018 the company laid off most of its employees, and headcount fell from 800 to fewer than 25.

In the meantime, the law had already moved. In March 2018 the SEC brought civil fraud charges against Theranos, Holmes and Balwani. According to the SEC, more than 700 million dollars had been raised from investors while false claims were made about the product. One claim was that the US Department of Defense was using the technology in combat situations, which turned out to be false. Another was that the company had a 100 million dollar revenue stream in 2014. In reality, it earned only 100,000 dollars that year. On 14 March 2018, Holmes settled with the SEC. She paid a 500,000 dollar penalty, returned 18.9 million shares and accepted a ten-year ban.

In June 2018, a federal grand jury charged Holmes and Balwani with wire fraud and conspiracy. Both pleaded not guilty. According to the indictment there were two schemes: one against investors and the other against doctors and patients. After the indictment Holmes stopped being CEO but remained chair of the board. In September 2018, with no buyer found, Theranos announced it was shutting down. Its remaining assets were to go to creditors.

Holmes's trial began on 31 August 2021, delayed by more than a year because of COVID-19 and Holmes's pregnancy. Holmes testified for seven days. She said staff had misled her about the technology and that Balwani dominated her. She also said Balwani did not force her to make false statements. Balwani denied the abuse allegations.

On 3 January 2022, the jury found Holmes guilty on four counts: three of wire fraud and one of conspiracy. All were related to investors. She was acquitted on four counts related to patients. On the remaining three counts the jury could not reach a decision, a mistrial was declared, and the prosecution dropped them.

Balwani's trial began in March 2022. In July he was found guilty on all 12 counts and sentenced to 12 years and 11 months in prison. Holmes received 11 years and 3 months, and together they were ordered to pay 452 million dollars in restitution.

articleEn: So the question remains: why did people believe? One reason was Holmes's personal connections. Part of Theranos's credibility came from the backing of influential people. Names such as Kissinger, Shultz, Mattis and DeVos, all linked to the US cabinet, were associated with the company. The board was criticized for being filled mostly with people from diplomatic and military backgrounds.

The second reason was money. Between 2004 and 2016, the cash available for private equity and venture capital grew from 400 billion dollars to 1.5 trillion dollars. In such an era, investors were under pressure to put their money somewhere. In this case, weak due diligence and fraudulent business practices did the damage.

The third reason was secrecy. According to employees, the company had a culture of secrecy and fear, and those who objected were usually marginalized or fired. And the biggest gap was peer review. For a technology carrying such a huge claim, no peer-reviewed research had appeared by 2015.

Now to where things stand today. Holmes arrived on 30 May 2023 at the Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, Texas, a minimum-security prison. She appealed to the Ninth Circuit, but in February 2025 the court rejected her arguments and upheld the conviction and sentence. Then in March 2026 Judge Davila reduced her sentence by 12 months. The reasons given were revised guidelines and the fact that investors' personal losses had not been proven. According to a September 2026 Bureau of Prisons notification, Holmes is to be moved to the Austin Transitional Center on 23 August 2027. Her scheduled release date is 22 February 2030. It is not clear whether her sentence will be shortened further after the halfway house, and no reason was given.

The story also inspired books and films. Carreyrou's Bad Blood came out in May 2018, followed by The Dropout podcast, HBO's The Inventor and a Hulu miniseries, in which Amanda Seyfried played Holmes. In October 2026 the documentary You Can See Everything was released, showing the weeks before she went to prison. It is also said that the case created a stigma for female founders. According to Erin Griffith, women entrepreneurs are often compared to Holmes.
Now the question is how much Holmes knew. She said Balwani dominated her, but that he did not force her to make false statements.

So what is the lesson? Big names and big valuations are not proof. When a company makes claims in a field like health, independent testing and peer review are essential. Tevanian voiced doubts on the board about the company's finances and technology, yet his departure at the end of 2007 was bitter. The story reminds us how important it is to ask questions.

shorts.titleEn: One 2-Hour Meeting That Built Theranos' Famous Board
shorts.text: صرف دو گھنٹے کی meeting، اور ایک بڑا نام Theranos کے ساتھ جڑ گیا۔ July 2011 میں Elizabeth Holmes کی ملاقات سابق US Secretary of State George Shultz سے کرائی گئی۔ دو گھنٹے کی بات چیت کے بعد وہ Theranos کے board of directors میں شامل ہو گئے۔ اس کے بعد تین سال میں Shultz نے تقریباً تمام outside directors کو متعارف کرانے میں مدد کی۔ board میں Henry Kissinger، William Perry، Sam Nunn اور Bill Frist جیسے نام تھے۔ بعد میں اسے امریکی corporate تاریخ کا سب سے شاندار board کہا گیا۔ لیکن اسی board پر تنقید بھی ہوئی کہ اس میں زیادہ تر diplomatic یا military background والے لوگ تھے۔ کیا بڑے نام ہی کافی تھے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Sirf do ghantay ki meeting, aur aik bara naam Theranos ke saath jur gaya. July 2011 mein Elizabeth Holmes ki mulaqat sabiq US Secretary of State George Shultz se karai gayi. Do ghantay ki baat cheet ke baad woh Theranos ke board of directors mein shamil ho gaye. Is ke baad teen saal mein Shultz ne taqreeban tamam outside directors ko mutaarif karane mein madad ki. board mein Henry Kissinger, William Perry, Sam Nunn aur Bill Frist jaise naam thay. Baad mein ise Amreeki corporate tareekh ka sab se shandar board kaha gaya. Lekin isi board par tanqeed bhi hui ke is mein zyada tar diplomatic ya military background walay log thay. Kya bare naam hi kafi thay? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: In July 2011 a two-hour meeting brought George Shultz onto the Theranos board. Here is how an all-star board was built, and why it was criticized.

shorts.titleEn: The Tip That Started Theranos' Unraveling
shorts.hook: Aik tip ne sab badal diya
shorts.text: دوستو، ایک tip نے پوری کہانی بدل دی۔ John Carreyrou، Wall Street Journal کے investigative journalist، کو ایک medical expert نے tip دی۔ اس expert کو Theranos کی Edison blood testing device مشکوک لگ رہی تھی۔ Carreyrou نے خاموشی سے کئی مہینے investigation کی۔ انہوں نے سابق employees سے بات کی اور company کی documents حاصل کیں۔ ان کے اہم sources میں Tyler Shultz بھی تھے، جو 2013 سے 2014 تک Theranos میں کام کرتے رہے۔ دلچسپ بات یہ کہ وہ George Shultz کے پوتے تھے، جو اس وقت Theranos کے director تھے۔ Tyler نے پہلے اپنے خدشات company management تک پہنچائے۔ جب بات نہ بنی، تو انہوں نے کیا کیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Dostو, aik tip ne poori kahani badal di. John Carreyrou, Wall Street Journal ke investigative journalist, ko aik medical expert ne tip di. Is expert ko Theranos ki Edison blood testing device mushkook lag rahi thi. Carreyrou ne khamoshi se kai mahine investigation ki. Unhon ne sabiq employees se baat ki aur company ki documents hasil kiin. Un ke aham sources mein Tyler Shultz bhi thay, jo 2013 se 2014 tak Theranos mein kaam karte rahe. Dilchasp baat yeh ke woh George Shultz ke pote thay, jo us waqt Theranos ke director thay. Tyler ne pehle apne khadshaat company management tak pohanchaye. Jab baat na bani, to unhon ne kya kiya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: A medical expert's tip led WSJ reporter John Carreyrou to investigate Theranos. Tyler Shultz, grandson of a Theranos director, became a key source.

shorts.titleEn: $600 Million Gone: Who Lost Money in Theranos?
shorts.text: 600 million dollars سے زیادہ ایک company میں ڈوب گئے۔ May 2018 میں John Carreyrou نے رپورٹ کیا کہ امریکی business اور government کے بڑے لوگوں نے Theranos میں اتنی رقم کھو دی۔ Walton family کے 150 million، Rupert Murdoch کے 121 million، Betsy DeVos کے 100 million اور Cox family کے 100 million شامل تھے۔ اس سے پہلے May 2017 میں تقریباً 99 فیصد shareholders نے company سے معاہدہ کیا۔ تمام موجودہ اور ممکنہ مقدمات ختم ہوئے، اور بدلے میں نئے preferred shares ملے۔ Holmes نے اپنی کچھ equity بھی چھوڑ دی۔ مگر September 2018 میں company کی liquidation نے یہ تمام investments بے قیمت کر دیں۔ کیا یہ معاہدہ company کو بچا سکا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: 600 million dollars se zyada aik company mein doob gaye. May 2018 mein John Carreyrou ne report kiya ke Amriki business aur government ke bare logon ne Theranos mein itni raqam kho di. Walton family ke 150 million, Rupert Murdoch ke 121 million, Betsy DeVos ke 100 million aur Cox family ke 100 million shamil thay. Is se pehle May 2017 mein taqreeban 99 feesad shareholders ne company se muaahida kiya. Tamam maujooda aur mumkina muqadmaat khatam hue, aur badle mein naye preferred shares milay. Holmes ne apni kuch equity bhi chhor di. Magar September 2018 mein company ki liquidation ne yeh tamam investments be qeemat kar din. Kya yeh muaahida company ko bacha saka? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: Investors including the Walton family, Rupert Murdoch, Betsy DeVos and the Cox family lost over $600 million in Theranos. See how a 2017 deal failed to save it.
